bib.title: Deep Learning (Chapter 10, An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python)

question: What are neural networks, CNNs and RNNs, how are they fit, and when is deep learning preferable to simpler statistical models?
hypothesis: Simpler models (linear, lasso) should be tried first; deep learning pays off with very large samples and low interpretability needs.
contributions: Introduces single and multilayer networks, CNNs, RNNs, backpropagation, SGD, dropout and double descent
Worked comparisons against lasso/linear/AR baselines on Hitters, IMDb, NYSE, MNIST

Hitters NN comparison on a single random split with 87 test points, no repeats; authors note results vary a lot by split
Lab uses test set as validation for Hitters and NYSE
Written early 2020: state-of-the-art figures (CIFAR100 75%, IMDb 95%) are dated; no transformers or attention covered
Comparison against trees, boosting or random forests on tabular data is not run; only linear models and lasso
practices: Try simpler models (linear, lasso) as well and choose on the performance/complexity tradeoff (Occam's razor), p.426-427
Prefer deep learning when the training set is extremely large and interpretability is not a priority, p.427
Control overfitting with early stopping, ridge/lasso penalties, dropout and data augmentation, p.427-431
Use a validation set for early stopping; do not early-stop on test data, p.462
Standardise inputs before lasso/NN since scale matters, p.438 and p.444
Reuse pretrained CNN layers (weight freezing) for small-data problems, p.412
Do not rely on double descent; regularise or early stop instead, p.435
Use a straw-man baseline (yesterday's value) for forecasting, p.423
Do not report selection-biased summary tables from a model chosen on the same data, p.426
